text: Good morning, Class 11-B. Ms. Rao is at a science teachers' training programme today, so I am taking your class. Her message: keep your NCERT book open at page 38. We will solve Example 3.8 together, then you will try a short program yourself. Today's topic is projectile motion. Keep one question in mind: at what angle should you throw a ball to make it go farthest? Make a guess now.

args.text:
- thrown or launched
- then moves under gravity alone

text: Let's start with a fielder throwing the ball to the keeper. Once it leaves the hand, the only thing acting on it is gravity. We are ignoring air resistance.

args.text: A projectile is anything thrown or launched that then moves under gravity alone.

text: That is a projectile: anything thrown or launched that then moves under gravity alone.
A football kick is one too. So is the arc of water from a hose, where every drop follows the same curved path.
Open your book at page 38, where this definition sits. Make sense?

args.title: Two motions at the same time: horizontal and vertical are independent

args.text: Two motions at the same time

- sideways: no push, so the speed stays the same
- up and down: gravity, g = 9.8 m/s²

text: Here are the two motions. Think of a ball hit from the boundary. Sideways, nothing pushes or pulls it, so its horizontal speed stays the same all the way. Up and down, gravity acts on it, pulling down at 9.8 metres per second every second.
The book gives this in Equation 3.35: ax is zero, and ay is minus g.

The up-and-down motion is the one that slows going up and speeds up coming down. So the two motions happen at the same time but never mix. Each direction can be solved on its own, with its own simple rule. That is the big idea: horizontal and vertical motion are independent. Clear so far?

args.title: Splitting the launch speed: ux = u cos θ and uy = u sin θ

text: When the ball leaves the hand at an angle, the launch speed u has two parts. Here u is the launch speed and θ is the angle above the horizontal.
Take u = 20 m/s at 30 degrees. Here is the picture.

args.items: box:Launch speed u | arrow:split | result:ux and uy

text: Here is the rule for the sideways part, ux = u cos θ. Let's put in the numbers.

args.text: - ux = u cos θ = 20 × cos 30° = 17.3 m/s

args.items: box:ux = u cos θ | good:sideways, steady

text: So the sideways speed is 17.3 m/s. Next is the upward part, uy = u sin θ.

args.text: - uy = u sin θ = 20 × sin 30° = 10 m/s

args.items: box:uy = u sin θ | good:upwards, changes

text: So the upward speed is 10 m/s, and this is the part gravity will slow down. Common mistake: using 20 m/s for both directions. The full speed does not go sideways or up. Takeaway: split the launch speed first, then use each part on its own.

text: Here are the steps for any projectile problem.

args.label: Write down what is given: u, θ and g

text: First, write down what is given: u, θ and g.

args.label: Split u into ux and uy

text: Second, split u into ux and uy, as we just did.
Third, the maximum height is h = uy² over 2g.

args.label: Time of flight: T = 2 uy / g

text: Fourth, the time of flight is T = 2 uy over g.
Fifth, the range is R = u² sin 2θ over g.

args.label: Check the answer against the book

text: Sixth, check the answer against the book.
Let's use our 20 m/s example, where uy is 10 m/s, and work the height first. This is the formula with our numbers in place. Now the top of the fraction.
Ten squared is 100, so the top of the fraction is 100.
Two times 9.8 is 19.6, so the bottom is 19.6.

100 divided by 19.6 gives 5.1, so the maximum height is 5.1 m, the highest point of the throw. Why uy and not u? Gravity only acts up and down, so only the upward part matters for the height. Next, the time in the air, T = 2 uy over g.
Twice uy is 20, which goes on the top.

20 divided by 9.8 gives 2.04, so the time in the air is 2.04 s. Going up and coming down take the same time, because the path is symmetrical. Now the range, R = u² sin 2θ over g. We can also multiply the sideways speed by the time in the air.
17.3 times 2.04 gives 35.3, so the range is 35.3 m. The shortcut uses u squared and sin 2θ, so let's check it. Here are the first two pieces.
u squared is 400, and sin 60 is 0.866.

400 times 0.866 is 346.4, and 346.4 divided by 9.8 gives 35.3 again. Both routes agree, so the shortcut is a good check. Takeaway: height and time come from uy, and the range comes from the sideways speed times the time in the air, or from the shortcut.
This is Example 3.8 on page 40 of your book.
A cricket ball is thrown at 28 m/s, 30 degrees above the horizontal.
We need three answers: the maximum height, the time to return to the same level, and the distance. Write the givens first.
Those are our starting numbers. Part (a) is the height, and it needs uy first.
So uy is 14 m/s, the upward part of the throw. Now the height, h = uy² over 2g.
14 squared is 196, which goes on the top.
196 divided by 19.6 gives 10.0, so the maximum height is 10.0 m. Part (b) is the time to return to the same level, T = 2 uy over g.
Twice 14 is 28.
28 divided by 9.8 gives 2.86, which rounds to about 2.9 s. Part (c) is the distance, R = u² sin 2θ over g, with 2θ equal to 60 degrees. Let's get the pieces first.
28 squared is 784, and sin 60 is 0.866.
784 times 0.866 gives 678.9, so that is the top of the range fraction.
678.9 divided by 9.8 gives 69.3, so the distance is about 69 m.
That gives 10.0 m, 2.9 s and 69 m, which matches the book's answers on page 40. Now let's check it with code.

args.code:
import math
g = 9.8
u = 28
theta = math.radians(30)
ux = u * math.cos(theta)
uy = u * math.sin(theta)
h = uy ** 2 / (2 * g)
T = 2 * uy / g
R = ux * T
print("Maximum height:", round(h, 1), "m")
print("Time of flight:", round(T, 1), "s")
print("Range:", round(R), "m")

text: Here is the program that checks these three numbers. Let's run it and see.

Range: 69 m

text: Good, the program printed three lines: the maximum height, 10.0 m; the time of flight, 2.9 s; and the range, 69 m. They match our hand working and the book's answers on page 40.

args.title: Range against launch angle
args.brief:
Plots: range in metres against launch angle, from 0° to 90°, for u = 20 m/s with no air resistance.
Points: 0°: 0.0, 15°: 20.4, 30°: 35.3, 45°: 40.8, 60°: 35.3, 75°: 20.4, 90°: 0.0

text: Here is the graph of range against launch angle, for a ball thrown at 20 m/s with no air resistance. Across the bottom is the launch angle, from 0 to 90 degrees. Up the side is the range in metres. A line graph fits because the angle changes smoothly, so the curve shows the whole pattern at once. Before I move the marker, guess the range at 15 degrees.
Here, at 15 degrees, the range is 20.4 m.
Your guess may have been higher or lower, and that is fine. Now the top of the curve, which answers our opening question. Guess the angle where the range is largest.
Here, at the peak, 45 degrees, the range is 40.8 m.
That is the highest point on the whole curve. Last one: guess the range at 90 degrees, where the ball goes straight up.
Here, at 90 degrees, the range is 0.0 m.
The ball rises and falls back to the same spot, so it travels no distance sideways. Here is the formula behind the curve.

args.text:
- R = u² sin 2θ / g
- highest at 45 degrees

text: Takeaway: the range rises from 15 degrees, peaks at 45 degrees, and falls back to zero at 90 degrees. Which part of the curve surprised you most?

args.title: Why 45 degrees gives the maximum range

text: Look at the formula again: R = u² sin 2θ / g. For one throw, u and g stay fixed, so the only thing that changes is sin 2θ. Sine is largest, equal to 1, when its angle is 90 degrees.

args.text: sin 2θ is largest (= 1) when 2θ = 90°, so θ = 45°.

text: So 2θ must be 90 degrees, which makes θ equal to 45 degrees.
Let's test it with two angles that add up to 90, starting with 15 degrees.
Twice 15 is 30, and the sine of 30 is 0.5.
400 times 0.5 is 200, and 200 divided by 9.8 gives 20.4. So 15 degrees gives 20.4 m. Now 75 degrees.
Twice 75 is 150, and the sine of 150 is also 0.5, the same value as before.
So 75 degrees also gives 20.4 m. Now the peak, 45 degrees.
Twice 45 is 90, and the sine of 90 is exactly 1, its largest possible value.
400 divided by 9.8 gives 40.8, the largest range of the three angles. Takeaway: sin 2θ peaks at 90 degrees, so 45 degrees throws farthest, and angles that add up to 90 share the same range.
Book Example 3.6 on page 40 proves this same symmetry, so compare its proof with our numbers.

Our opening question was which angle throws farthest on flat ground. The answer is 45 degrees, because sin 2θ is largest there. Remember three things: horizontal and vertical motion are independent, split u into ux and uy first, and use R = u² sin 2θ / g for the range.
